 Log in Rays finish off Guards to set up World Series clash vs. Crew
 5:23 AM UTC Keegan Matheson
 Share share-square--:R1qlq: ST. PETERSBURG -- The Rays are headed to the World Series, champions of the American League after a night this team and these fans will never forget. 
 It was 18 years ago on this exact date -- Oct. 19, 2008 -- when the Rays punched their ticket to their first World Series, and Monday’s 7-3 win over the Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS is sending them back for another shot at their first title in franchise history.
 World Series Presented by Capital One, Game 1, Friday, 8 p.m. ET on FOX/FOX Deportes/FOX One 
 “Tampa is the best!” Junior Caminero  shouted on the field after the game. “Tampa gave me the opportunity to come play here. Tampa! This is for you! Come on now, come on, let’s go!”
 The 2026 World Series  will crown a first-time champion either way as the Rays face the Brewers, who swept the back-to-back defending champion Dodgers in the NLCS. The Brewers have never won the World Series since joining MLB in 1969 as the Seattle Pilots and the Rays, who joined MLB in ’98, are in the same boat. Coming off the Dodgers’ dominance, a new day will dawn. 
 Now, the Rays will catch their breath and travel to Milwaukee for  Game 1 of the World Series at American Family Field, with first pitch scheduled for Friday at 8 p.m. ET. By then, the Brewers will have been off for eight days, going back to their NLCS clinch on Oct. 15.
 “This group, they’ve been a complete joy to be around all season long. I know they’re very, very motivated,” said Rays manager Kevin Cash. “I heard the line that we don’t have any Hall of Famers in that room right now -- we might, but not yet. But I can assure you we have a lot of gamers, and we’re excited to get up there to Milwaukee.”
 Caminero's two-run shot off the left-field foul pole in the seventh inning is an instant classic, the type of moment that will stick with the young superstar for years. Tropicana Field hasn’t been that loud since the Rays’ run in 2008, and Caminero is not just one of the best hitters on the planet, he is a showman, an entertainer, the face of the Tampa Bay Rays.
 Stopping in front of first base, Caminero stood and turned to his dugout, the stadium shaking around him. He rounded the bases as his teammates spilled onto the field , and then, just inches before crossing home plate, he stopped again. He pointed at former Rays great Randy Arozarena, seated behind home plate, and they both hit Arozarena’s signature pose, arms crossed defiantly in front of their chests.
 You can’t script these moments. 
 “I want to cry right now because I’ve put in a lot of work for this team, to support this city,” Caminero said. “My family out there, my wife, my mom, my father, my little brother, my daughter, Valentina. I’m very happy. This is for the Dominican Republic, right here.”

 Caminero brought the house down, but  Richie Palacios  lit it on fire in the second inning with a two-run double that’s going to live on Rays highlight reels for years. The Rays so often wear the label of the gritty, scrappy team, and this at-bat was the very definition of it.
 Palacios was facing left-hander Tim Herrin, but lefties have carved him up in 2026, holding Palacios to a .158 average and .478 OPS. The early pitches in this at-bat made those numbers seem generous, with Palacios fighting off pitches and trying to check a couple of swings, but then it finally happened.

 Sign up As that ball bounced into the right-center gap and Palacios raced into second base, his helmet tumbling into the dirt behind him, he turned back to his dugout and let out an incredible howl. It’s the biggest moment of his baseball life. It’s the biggest win of so many of their baseball lives.
 By the time Yandy Díaz  launched his two-run shot to left field in the bottom of the eighth, immediately erasing any threat the Guardians had built in the top half, Rays fans were delirious. Chants of “Yandy! Yandy! Yandy!” rained down until he obliged, bursting out of the dugout for a curtain call .
 “It feels like I’m on top of the world,” Diaz said through interpreter Kevin Vera. “Hopefully this time around, it’s for us to win.”
 By the time the dam burst in Game 6, the Rays were simply the better team. Even in a tight series between such similar teams, the pressure had been building and building. The Rays kept nailing the cornerstones of their identity, from the speed of Chandler Simpson to the incredible defense of Taylor Walls and their rock solid pitching. Eventually, with all of that leaning on another team, something cracks. That’s why they play 162 games … and then some.

 Freddy Peralta dominated the Guardians again, too, throwing 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball coming off six shutout innings in his Game 2 win. It was a pitching mismatch from the very beginning, as the Guardians went with a bullpen game led by Shawn Armstrong, but Cleveland just couldn’t get any of their momentum to snowball offensively. This lineup, led by José Ramírez , was scorching hot down the stretch and in the ALCS, but the Rays’ pitching staff is built to snuff out streaks.
 Peralta was named the ALCS MVP , and even after the celebrations died down, he couldn’t stop smiling and shaking his head. That MVP trophy might be on the pillow next to his head tonight.
 “This is unbelievable,” Peralta said. “I think I have to see it when I go home tonight and start thinking about it, because I am still in shock. I don't believe it.”
 Your browser does not support HTML5 video tag. Click here to view original asset This is why the Rays are great. They suck all of the oxygen out of the room and don’t leave any left for the other team to breathe. The Guardians are a very good ball club coming off an excellent run, including that amazing comeback in the ALDS against the White Sox, but they’re not the Rays, at least not this year. 
 “It’s a great baseball team. Great baseball teams win big games,” said Guardians outfielder Steven Kwan. “They played defense better than us, they hit better than us, they pitched better than us. We didn’t beat ourselves, we got beat. As a competitor, you can live with that. I’m disappointed, but that’s a great team over there.”
 The Guardians have so much to build on from this run , even if that’s going to be no consolation in the coming days and weeks. Built around Ramírez, the longtime face of their franchise, they have one of the best young outfielders in the American League in rookie Chase DeLauter and are stacked with young pitching talent, headlined by Gavin Williams, Parker Messick and closer Cade Smith.
 They’ll have every opportunity to get back here -- and find a path through the ALCS -- but  the longest title drought in Major League Baseball is going to stretch into its 78th year. The Guardians have not won the World Series since 1948, despite playing in four since (‘54, ‘95, ‘97, ‘16) and playing in seven ALCS. 
 The Rays have been twice before, first in 2008 and later in ‘20. This feels different, though, especially for those who were around for the last one. Played during the COVID-19 pandemic, that World Series was centralized at Arlington’s Globe Life Field with only a quarter of the stadium full. This time, it’s in their house, and their house is loud.
 What you need to know about the 2026 World Series 
 “2020 was as special as any season I've been a part of,” Cash said. “But saying that, we didn't have 40,000 people behind us. I’m excited to see what those 40,000 people can bring on Games 3, 4 and 5, for sure. I thought the ALDS crowd, Game 1, was the best crowd I've ever heard. This crowd tonight, they might have been a little bit better.”
 Monday night belonged to the Rays, and in the American League, 2026 belongs to the Rays. We haven’t seen Tropicana Field this full and this loud in a long time. We haven’t seen a Rays team this good in a long time, and now, they’re four wins away from history.
